html:
From the mid 19th century until the 1930s, millions of migrants from southern China came to Malaya, mostly to work in tin mines, on plantations and in trade. Many returned home, but large numbers stayed.

They came from Fujian and Guangdong and spoke Hokkien, Cantonese, Hakka, Teochew and other tongues. Smaller groups, the Peranakan or Straits Chinese, had settled in Malacca and Penang much earlier. Secret societies and clan associations organised their lives.

By 1931 Chinese made up about two in five of the people of British Malaya, including the Straits Settlements. Their place in the nation became the central question of Malaysian politics, from the Malayan Union to the riots of 1969 and the New Economic Policy.
